plan.title: What Really Caused the 2008 Financial Crisis
plan.description: The story of the 2008 financial crisis, from the US housing boom and subprime mortgages to securitization, the fall of Lehman Brothers and the government response. It explains how risky lending turned into a global crash.

beats.narration: In September 2008, one of Wall Street's oldest banks went bankrupt in a single weekend. Within weeks, the world's financial system was close to freezing. How did a housing boom end here?
beats.speaker: narrator

beats.narration: It began with cheap money. Interest rates were low, credit was easy, and rules were light. Homes seemed to only gain value, so more people wanted to buy, and banks wanted to lend.

Then lenders went further. Subprime mortgages went to borrowers with poor credit. Many loans skipped the old checks of collateral, credit history and character, because banks could simply sell the loans on.
In 2005 and 2006, about $1.2 trillion of subprime mortgages were made. Roughly 80 percent of them were securitized. That one word is the heart of the story.

props.label: Subprime mortgages made in 2005-2006, about 80% securitized

beats.narration: Here is how it worked. Borrowers paid their mortgages. Banks pooled thousands of loans together. Investors bought securities backed by those payments, and rating agencies stamped them as safe.

But there was a flaw. Lenders who sold loans no longer cared if borrowers could repay. Careful underwriting faded, and risk was passed along. Financial engineers then stacked complex products on top, like squared and synthetic CDOs.

props.text: If you can sell the risk, why care who repays?

beats.narration: When housing prices stopped rising, the trouble started. Borrowers could not pay or refinance. Securities once called safe lost value, and nobody knew who was holding the losses.

clip_queries: foreclosure sign in front of house

beats.narration: The crisis began in the summer of 2007. Then Countrywide, Bear Stearns, IndyMac, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac all failed or were rescued, one after another. Pressure built on every big bank.
On September 15, 2008, Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy. It held $639 billion in assets and $619 billion in debt, and had almost 26,000 employees. It was the largest bankruptcy in U.S. history.

props.image_query: Wall Street New York stock exchange

beats.narration: Regulators had scrambled all weekend to find a buyer. Bank of America walked away. Then the Barclays deal fell through. The government refused to guarantee Lehman, and it fell.
Panic spread. A money market fund broke the buck, meaning it could not pay investors a full dollar per dollar invested. A run on those funds followed, and the Fed promised to guarantee their assets.

props.definition: When a money market fund cannot pay investors a full dollar for each dollar they invested.

beats.narration: The government answered with trillions in rescue efforts. Congress passed the Troubled Asset Relief Program, called TARP, with $700 billion to stabilize the financial system. The Treasury, the Fed and the FDIC added emergency programs.

props.label: Authorized for TARP to stabilize the financial system

beats.narration: The Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission later concluded the crisis was avoidable. It blamed widespread failures in financial regulation and corporate governance, fueled by low rates, easy credit, scant regulation and toxic mortgages.

props.text: The collapse of the housing bubble, fueled by low interest rates, easy and available credit, scant regulation, and toxic mortgages, was the spark that ignited the crisis.

beats.narration: So the cause was not one villain. It was easy money, loans nobody checked, risk sold on and hidden, and weak oversight. When people stop owning their risk, everyone eventually pays.

mismatch_scenes: beat 10 (timeline): its narration never says ['Rescue talks begin', 'Lehman files for bankruptcy', 'Fed bails out AIG']

accuracy.reason: Most figures match the notes ($1.2T, 80%, $639B/$619B, $700B, 15 Sept). But "went bankrupt in a single weekend" is loose, and "Fed bails out AIG" on Sept 16 is compressed. The timeline also puts "Rescue talks begin" under "Sept 2008" with no day.

coverage.reason: It covers the boom, subprime, securitization, Lehman and TARP. It omits rating-agency conflicts, leverage, and the Fed's rate or QE actions. It gives no lasting effects (recession, unemployment, Dodd-Frank), and it says the 'trillions' response was in the notes' words but unspecified.

structure.reason: Clear chronological chapters (boom, subprime, securitization, crash, Lehman, response) lead to a closing synthesis. There is minor repetition of causes in beats 13 and 14.

hook_ending.reason: The opening is a dramatic event, but the closing question "How did a housing boom end here?" is awkward. The ending line is decent but moralizing and slightly generic.

tone.reason: Plain, accessible explainer voice suited to a US general audience, though it sometimes reads like a report.

visuals.reason: Scene types vary well (diagram, stat, timeline, definition, quote). The stat and counter use real numbers and the queries fit. The generic Wall Street image for Lehman is weak.

originality.reason: Specifics such as the three C's, squared and synthetic CDOs, and breaking the buck add some interest. Overall it is a standard retelling, and the ending is cliché-ish.

instructions.reason: It is told as a story from the housing boom and includes subprime, securitization, Lehman and the government response. The length is near target at roughly 440 words.

language.reason: Fluent and grammatical, with a few awkward lines such as "How did a housing boom end here?" and "Homes seemed to only gain value".

defects.quote: How did a housing boom end here?
defects.issue: The hook's closing question is clumsy and vague, and does not create real tension.

defects.quote: went bankrupt in a single weekend
defects.issue: Lehman's troubles had built for months, and the rescue talks ran over a weekend. The phrasing oversimplifies.

defects.quote: Countrywide, Bear Stearns, IndyMac, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac all failed or were rescued
defects.issue: Bear Stearns was sold to JPMorgan with Fed support, and Fannie and Freddie were put into conservatorship. Calling them all 'failed or rescued' is vague, and Bear is not explained.

defects.quote: rating agencies stamped them as safe
defects.issue: The role of the rating agencies and the conflicts of interest are not explained. Leverage is entirely absent.

defects.quote: The government answered with trillions in rescue efforts.
defects.issue: The Fed's actions are vague, and the script gives no lasting effects such as the Great Recession, job losses or Dodd-Frank.

defects.quote: fueled by low rates, easy credit, scant regulation and toxic mortgages
defects.issue: The narration repeats the causes from the quote on screen and from beat 2, which is redundant.

defects.quote: Wall Street New York stock exchange
defects.issue: A generic image does not show Lehman, whose collapse is the narration's subject.
